strengths: Valuable and comprehensive dataset: DarkClusters-15K (15,000 clusters) is the largest benchmark dataset for galaxy cluster mass mapping with realistic lensing observations from multiple simulation frameworks, providing a significant community resource

Well-motivated physics-guided architecture: Principled integration of strong/weak gravitational lensing physics with diffusion models avoids rigid parametric assumptions while leveraging domain knowledge through properly formulated likelihood terms (Eqs. 10-14)

Rigorous technical execution: Sound mathematical formulation of gravitational lensing forward models, correct Jacobian calculations, proper Bayesian formulation via DAPS, and valid uncertainty quantification with well-calibrated posteriors (R²=0.99)

Comprehensive experimental validation: Thorough ablation studies (Fig. 4), multi-framework evaluation demonstrating generalization across redshifts and simulation frameworks, and comparison with appropriate baselines showing clear quantitative improvements

Practical efficiency and utility: Achieves minute-scale runtimes versus hours for traditional methods, enables fully automatic reconstruction without expert tuning, and demonstrates expert-level performance on real MACS 1206 cluster
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-structured paper with effective visualizations, commitment to release code and dataset, enabling future research and benchmarking
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Primary contribution is applying existing DDPM++ diffusion models with physics-based likelihood rather than developing fundamentally new methods; algorithmic innovation is modest
Mischaracterized contribution type: Paper presents as 'Algorithms/General' but more accurately represents 'Applied/Systems' + 'Datasets/Benchmarks', which affects assessment of novelty claims

Insufficient real-data validation: Dataset is entirely simulation-based with only one real cluster (MACS 1206) validated; light-traces-mass assumption shows only moderate correlation (PCC 0.58-0.65) even in own dataset, raising questions about real-world applicability

Limited generalization analysis: Lacks depth on why simulation-trained priors work for reality; testing restricted to cosmological simulations without evaluation on different cluster types (cool-core vs. non-cool-core), mass scales, or morphologies

Incomplete ablation studies: Missing analyses on photometry-conditioning quantification, sensitivity to observation noise levels, and sensitivity to key hyperparameters despite claims of reduced tuning

Insufficient failure case analysis: No discussion of failure modes, edge cases (merging clusters, highly irregular morphologies), or robustness to real observational systematics (PSF variations, background estimation)

Venue scope concerns: Specialized astrophysics application of inverse problems with limited connection to core computer vision; more appropriate for astronomy or physics-informed ML venues rather than ECCV
Incomplete computational characterization: GPU/memory requirements not specified; no analysis of how performance scales with cluster complexity or observation quality

Limited theoretical understanding: Minimal explanation of what diffusion model learns about mass distributions, why this particular physics+diffusion formulation works, or how to predict generalization; mode collapse not discussed

Comparison context issues: Napier et al. [37] uses 2D methods while this is 3D; claims about expert tuning but this method requires careful hyperparameter tuning (Appendix B); baseline methods use different assumptions

Principled integration of physics-based constraints (strong/weak lensing forward models) into a diffusion-based framework, with proper uncertainty calibration (R²=0.99)
Comprehensive ablation study demonstrating the necessity of both strong and weak lensing constraints for accurate reconstruction
Generalization testing across multiple redshifts and simulation frameworks (IllustrisTNG and SIMBA)
Clear presentation of methodology and reasonable experimental design for simulated data evaluation
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the approach applies established diffusion models (DAPS) and standard gravitational lensing physics without fundamental innovation; essentially combines existing components

Validation restricted to simulated data only; no testing on real observational data despite claims about upcoming surveys; critical assumptions (light-traces-mass) violated in simulations themselves (PCC only 0.58-0.65)
Modest empirical improvements; while PSNR gains are measurable, visual differences from Napier et al. in Figure 5 are not striking, and real scientific impact of improvements is unclear
Poor fit for ECCV: this is fundamentally an astrophysics application paper without novel computer vision methodology; diffusion models are applied as-is without CV-specific innovation

Severe real-world applicability concerns: Appendix C reveals the fundamental light-traces-mass assumption is violated due to massive dark matter clumps; unclear how well results transfer to real heterogeneous observational data with different noise, systematics, and physical properties

Incomplete experimental validation: generalization tested only across redshifts within same frameworks (no cross-framework generalization); no comparison with other recent deep learning mass reconstruction methods; missing hyperparameter sensitivity analysis

Dataset limitations inadequately addressed: both simulations may share systematic biases; mass distribution is skewed toward high-mass clusters; limited diversity in simulation frameworks; transferability to real surveys not demonstrated
Missing practical deployment analysis: computational costs only vaguely mentioned ('minutes') without concrete benchmarks; unclear feasibility for operational survey-scale processing

Overstated claims in abstract and conclusion; claims of 'fully automated' method and 'strengthening our tools for probing the Universe' are not sufficiently supported by simulation-only validation on systems with known fundamental limitations
Key limitations relegated to appendices (light-traces-mass analysis); failure case analysis absent; limited discussion of when/why the method succeeds or fails

strengths: Novel physics-guided diffusion methodology that integrates weak/strong lensing with learned priors through DAPS algorithm, demonstrating a creative approach to inverse problems that could inspire future work
DARKCLUSTERS-15K: largest benchmark dataset of its kind with 15,000 simulated clusters from multiple simulation frameworks, with commitment to public release enabling future research
Fully automated method requiring no expert tuning, achieving significant practical speedup (minutes vs hours) with strong quantitative results (PSNR 33.3 vs 26.0 for competing methods)

Rigorous experimental validation including ablation studies clearly demonstrating necessity of both strong and weak lensing, uncertainty calibration tests (R²=0.99), and generalization across simulation frameworks and redshifts
Well-calibrated uncertainty quantification essential for scientific applications, with demonstrated calibration quality and integration with posterior sampling
Integration of complementary weak lensing (outer regions), strong lensing (inner regions), and photometric observables is novel and principled
Clear mathematical exposition of gravitational lensing physics, diffusion models, and the technical approach with proper derivations and physical grounding
Successful demonstration on real galaxy cluster (MACS 1206) without manual intervention, showing practical applicability beyond simulations
weaknesses: Limited real-world validation: only one actual galaxy cluster example shown; additional examples would significantly strengthen practical applicability claims

Insufficient discussion of failure modes and edge cases: paper doesn't explore when method might struggle or provide guidance on failure detection

strengths: Well-motivated physics-guided approach that principally integrates gravitational lensing constraints with diffusion models through carefully designed loss functions
Substantial dataset contribution (DarkClusters-15K: 15,000 cluster observations) - largest of its kind with paired mass, photometry, and lensing observables from multiple simulations

Strong technical soundness with rigorous mathematical formulation, proper treatment of both weak and strong lensing regimes, and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates validated through reliability diagrams
Comprehensive experimental validation including thorough ablations (Figure 4), multiple meaningful baselines (Kaiser-Squires, Napier et al., UNet), and real-world application to MACS 1206
Significant practical advantages: fully automatic pipeline (no expert tuning), minutes-scale inference vs. hours for existing methods, uncertainty quantification essential for upcoming surveys
Clear presentation and good figure quality with detailed appendices supporting reproducibility and dataset construction
weaknesses: Questionable fit for ECCV: fundamentally an astrophysics application paper rather than computer vision research; limited contribution to CV/ML methodology that would benefit the vision community broadly
Limited methodological novelty: straightforward application of existing diffusion models with domain-specific loss functions; technical innovation over standard DAPS is incremental

Simulation-to-reality gap inadequately addressed: training exclusively on IllustrisTNG/SIMBA simulations with only one real cluster (MACS 1206) for validation; no systematic discussion of simulation biases or failure modes

Key design choices lack rigorous justification: RBF interpolation in Eq. 14 has no sensitivity analysis; photometry conditioning appears ad-hoc; light-traces-mass assumption (PCC~0.6) not deeply explored for robustness
Baseline comparisons potentially unfair: Napier et al. targets parametric models; recent deep-learning mass-mapping methods missing; UNet baseline configuration not optimized
Dataset limitations: restricted mass range (10^13.5-14 M☉), uniform sampling unrepresentative of real cluster distributions, training/test from same simulations may encode implicit assumptions

strengths: Comprehensive dataset contribution: DARKCLUSTERs-15K provides 15,000 realistic mock cluster observations derived from IllustrisTNG and SIMBA simulations with systematic lensing observables, addressing a real need in the field.

Solid methodology: Properly integrates physics-based gravitational lensing constraints with diffusion model priors through likelihood weighting, producing physically plausible reconstructions with quantified uncertainty.
Practical efficiency gains: Achieves inference in minutes rather than hours, and is fully automated without requiring manual tuning or cluster-specific expert configuration.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Includes proper baselines, ablation studies, uncertainty calibration validation, and analysis across different redshifts and simulation frameworks.
Well-executed technical presentation: Clear mathematical exposition of gravitational lensing formalism and integration with diffusion models; generally clear writing.
weaknesses: Poor venue alignment for ECCV: This is fundamentally an astrophysics application paper with limited computer vision or machine learning novelty. The core contribution is a straightforward application of existing diffusion models to a specialized domain, better suited for domain-specific venues (ApJ, MNRAS) or ML conferences.

Severely limited real-world validation: Training dataset consists entirely of simulations; only one real cluster (MACS 1206) is validated. Distribution shift between simulations and real observations not thoroughly analyzed. Insufficient to support claims of practical applicability to real astronomical surveys.

Incremental ML novelty: Uses diffusion models for inverse problems (well-established), conditions on lensing/photometry (straightforward), and applies existing DAPS algorithm [56]. The physics-conditioning mechanism (likelihood weighting) is standard. No novel generative modeling or reconstruction techniques introduced.

Unfair experimental comparisons: Different baselines use different input observables (Kaiser-Squires: WL only; Napier et al.: SL only; authors: both), confounding direct comparison. On real MACS 1206 data (Figure 6), performance is comparable to Napier et al., not clearly superior. Improvements on simulated data are marginal (typically <5% in most metrics).

Unaddressed critical assumption: Light-traces-mass assumption shows only moderate correlation (0.58-0.61) in Appendix D, indicating frequent violations. This limitation deserves prominence as it affects method validity, yet is buried in appendix. Implications for real cluster analysis not discussed.

Incomplete technical justification: Multiple approximations (linear weak lensing model, radial basis interpolation, ad-hoc geometric loss) and hyperparameter choices (λ_k via 'parameter sweeps') lack rigorous justification or sensitivity analysis. Noise models (SNR 0.01-0.1) for weak lensing seem unrealistically high.

Limited generalization analysis: Training exclusively on z_L=0.5 clusters but testing on z_L ∈ {0.2, 0.5, 1.0}. Systematic performance degradation across redshifts not explicitly reported. Concerns about transfer to real observational data remain.

Dataset homogeneity: 15,000 projections derived from only 600 unique clusters with 25 projections each. Limited diversity in cluster masses (majority in 10^13.5-14 M_☉ range). Unclear how this generalizes to broader cluster populations.

Overstated claims: Positions the work as 'first fully automated framework' and 'strengthening tools for probing the Universe,' but automation via engineering is not a scientific contribution, and real-world applicability remains undemonstrated with only single-cluster validation.

Missing critical analysis: No discussion of when practitioners should prefer this method over existing approaches, scaling to full-sky surveys, computational requirements for large-scale deployment, or systematic failure mode analysis. When does the method perform poorly?

strengths: Well-motivated physics-informed machine learning approach that elegantly integrates gravitational lensing constraints with diffusion models through principled Bayesian inference
Substantial and valuable dataset contribution: DARKCLUSTERS-15K contains 15,000 simulated clusters with realistic multi-wavelength observations from IllustrisTNG and SIMBA simulations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on simulated data including proper uncertainty calibration (reliability diagrams), meaningful ablation studies, and comparisons against multiple baselines

Significant practical advantages: fully automatic (no expert tuning), efficient inference (minutes vs. hours/days), better quantitative performance than baselines, and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates
Strong experimental rigor with quantitative metrics (PSNR, SSIM, PCC, RMSE) across different redshifts and simulation frameworks, demonstrating generalization capabilities
Excellent reproducibility commitment: authors promise code and dataset release with thorough documentation in appendices
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the method primarily applies existing techniques (diffusion models, DAPS, standard lensing equations) to a new domain without fundamental innovation

Critical real-world validation gap: only one real galaxy cluster (MACS 1206) tested with mostly qualitative comparison to Caminha et al.; quantitative validation lacks formal statistical testing and confidence intervals

Insufficient generalization study: trained exclusively on simulations; domain gap between simulations and real observations not thoroughly explored; moderate light-traces-mass correlation (PCC ~0.6) suggests fundamental limitations
Narrow training data scope: only 600 clusters used for train/val/test (from 15,000), trained at single redshift; potential overfitting to simulation assumptions not addressed
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Kaiser-Squires is weak (weak lensing only), UNet is strawman (no physics constraints), Napier et al. appears unfairly compared given different design assumptions
Missing ablation studies and sensitivity analysis: no ablation on architectural choices, loss weight sensitivity (λ_k), DAPS alternatives, or diffusion scheduler impact
Unexamined failure modes and robustness: no discussion of when method breaks down, sensitivity to atypical morphologies, simulation biases, or cosmological assumptions
Uncertainty quantification concerns: reliability calibration demonstrated on simulated test data may not transfer to real observations where simulations diverge from reality

Limited scope for ECCV venue: fundamentally an astrophysics application with domain-specific focus; algorithmic contributions not transferable to broader computer vision; better suited for astronomy or physics ML venues
